old_title: England v New Zealand: Nations Championship rugby union - live
new_title: England 37-12 New Zealand: Hosts storm to historic Nations Championship win over All Blacks - as it happened
old_text:
30 mins. The All Blacks lose the ball again, Vaa'i coughing up a McKenzie pass that for once had them nearly on the front foot. If you're up in the middle of the night to follow this in Aotearoa then you have my sympathies for what your team is serving up.
28 mins. On a scrum penalty advantage NZ move the ball again, but it's very lateral with McKenzie crabbing across the field to make it easy for the England defence. Nothing comes of it so the All Blacks will go again back from the penalty on the right touchline.
25 mins. The NZ threequarters finally have the chance to warm their hands with some clean possession from a lineout. They run a nice pattern, but England cover it with little issue before Jordan spurts the ball out of his hands out on the wing under zero pressure.
23 mins. Back England come, however, with Furback running the ball back with far too much ease, cantering 30 metres into the NZ half. McKenzie adds to the problems by tackling Atkinson off the ball and the England pack drive to the line from the resulting 5m lineout.
Coles drives over but the black defence engulfs him to hold the ball up.
20 mins. England stroll into the 22 again, but in the final phases the All Blacks are that little bit more keen at the breakdown and spoil possession, this time keeping the ball off the ground to turn it over. There's another small victory for the visitors when they win a scrum penalty to once again relive the pressure.
18 mins. McKenzie scrambles to gather the ball from a Slade grubber that once again has NZ under pressure in their 22. They are calm enough to reset the ball and clear to touch. But the relief doesn't last long as Scott Barrett is penalised or collapsing a post-lineout maul.
The All Blacks are getting thwacked pretty much everywhere and England should be fuming they are not further ahead.
15 mins. A clean lineout win from Itoje is moved quickly to Smith who finds another kick in behind for Joseph to chase. It's a decent foot race but Bauden Barrett is first to it.
13 mins. Sititi has a dart from the base of the scrum to set up an attack in the middle of the England half before Ref Berry blasts on his whistle as Heyes is suspected of a hip-drop tackle. The opportunity is wasted as Talyor overthrows the 5m lineout and Earl snaffles it. Van Poortvliet clears his lines.
10 mins. There's no real benefit from the penalty lineout as the NZ defence are first to the breakdown to win a penalty of their own for England holding on. Roigard punts the ball upfield and a handling error in midfield hands a scrum to the All Blacks in enemy territory.
8 mins. The trademark of England's attack recently has been the speed of recycling and then the absolute confidence to use the ball when presented to the backs. This is evident again on the latest possession before Furbank drills an exquisite 50:22 down the right touchline with barely 5 metres to play with.
5 mins. Possession is retained by England from the penalty and some fast recycling hand Fin Smith an age to pick an angled grubber in-goal that Slade grounds.
Conversion is pulled left, but still a great start by the home side.
3 mins. England have their first attacking platform from a scrum just inside the NZ half. Joseph takes a solid carry into the line on first phase and this is enough to get the visiting defence moving backwards. The next few phases feature a rumble up by Earl before the ball is moved across the field and a desperate defence is already offside.
2 mins. Jordie Barrett is this close to grasping a long clearing kick from McKenzie after the All Blacks received the kick off. However, it bumps off his fingertips under a mid-air challenge from Will Joseph.
Lewis Moody has joined the England team as they line up to face the haka. The home side move into a V formation to receive the challenge led by NZ captain Codie Taylor.
Moody sees off each England player in turn as he leaves the field with emotion clearly running high with each of them and he embraces them in turn. Quite the build up.
England
George Furbank; Cadan Murley, Henry Slade, Seb Atkinson, Will Joseph; Fin Smith, Jack van Poortvliet; Fin Baxter, Jamie George, Joe Heyes; Maro Itoje (capt), Alex Coles; Ollie Chessum, Ben Curry, Ben Earl.
Replacements: Luke Cowan-Dickie, Ellis Genge, Will Stuart, George Martin, Greg Fisilau, Henry Pollock, Ben Spencer, Marcus Smith.
New Zealand
Beauden Barrett; Will Jordan, Anton Lienert-Brown, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby; Damian McKenzie, Cam Roigard; Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (capt), Fletcher Newell; Scott Barrett, Fabian Holland; Tupou Vaa'i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi.
Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Anton Segner, Leicester Fainga'anuku, Cortez Ratima, Richie Mo'unga, Rieko Ioane.
Alastair Campbell has a book out called Persevilience, the title apparently a mash-up of perseverance and resilience (see what he did there) to form the worst compound noun since dorkburger. Although, one imagines the creator of the latter wasn't trying to make it "the word the world needs now" like Big Al is on the cover of his volume.
However hateful the word, a still injury ravaged New Zealand need to show some of it today as they attempt to shrug off their seventy-three years in the making dorkburgering in Cardiff last week.
Since 1996, where the All Blacks have played tests with no more than a 21-day gap they suffered defeat in 52 first-up fixtures, with only 18 of the follow-up matches being a loss. Fourteen of those next-up losses were against either South Africa (10) or Australia (4), and they have only lost two consecutive matches on their November tours on one occasion in 2021 (Ireland, then France). On the 31 occasions they followed a defeat with a win, the week one loss margin average is seven points (sound familiar?) and the week two win margin is 26.
Thus, history tells us that such a situation tends lead to a rage filled bounceback being the order of the day, but matching the historic 26 point next-up winning spread will be a tougher ask than usual. The Dave Rennie led 2026 All Blacks are not the team of yore, and that's before we consider their medical list, plus they must deliver it at SponsorDome Twickenham versus an England side on a decent run of form and results.
Exactly how good the home side's run is can be debated; they are more fluent, confident and organised in attack than at any time during Borthwick's tenure, but their wins this Autumn have come against an indisputably wretched Australia and a weak Japan. They are yet to be tested in defence and New Zealand's attacking shortcomings vs Wales will surely not be repeated; but the squad is settled and consistent, with their tails up and no small amount of power and ability.
The sun is out and there's a fascinating test match incoming.
new_text:
Right, thanks for joining Lee earlier and me for a few minutes. Now you just about have time to read Robert's match report before joining Lee for Ireland v South Africa:
If Kiwi fans thought last week's loss to Wales was painful this was arguably as bad in terms of the reputational damage. The home side were 19-0 up after just 36 minutes and had the game all but wrapped up within a couple of minutes of the restart when Ollie Chessum smashed his way over to claim his side's fourth try. From a margin of victory perspective this was England's biggest victory over New Zealand in the 121-year-old history of the fixture.
There were even occasions when the fabled silver fern was in some danger of being totally trashed, with almost three-quarters of the game taking place in New Zealand half. If anything it was England who more closely resembled the slick All Black sides of yesteryear, particularly in the first-half when tries from Henry Slade, Jack van Poortvliet and Ben Earl rewarded the hosts' purposeful approach play and seemingly greater desire.
England paying the penalty for the 45-21 defeat in South Africa, when they failed to get a bonus point, while France did get two when they lost 34-32 to New Zealand.
Guy Hornsby writes: "I know people will say NZ have been poor, and they have, but England didn't give them a sniff for a half. They controlled possession, were layered in attack and brutal in defence. With Fin Smith, Furbank and Slade, there's 3 that can play first receiver, and Atkinson followed up the Australia game with another really promising game at 12, where he's looking settled. We can only beat who is in front of us, and right across the 23, we've been really great. It does feel like things are falling into place, and our depth, bar perhaps at hooker, if we get an injury, is looking pretty good. The mix of dynamic attack and power is really coming together. Excellent performance. For the All Blacks? A lot of soul searching, they really didn't fire much of a shot."
England have a huge points difference of 159. But any France win over Argentina with a bonus point would knock them down to second. Ireland could beat South Africa ... and wind up in Friday's third-place final.
Sean Fitzpatrick closes the reaction out by laughing ruefully at the possibility of a rematch against England in next weekend's second-place final. New Zealand have had a chastening few months. Care said they were worse against England than against Wales - and the scoreboard suggests he was right. But was that about England being so good?
Genge talks about the bench, the importance of being in the 23, "You have to be happy for each other ... it's not possible to do it for 80. We're happy to play whatever the role is as long as we're winning."
Hello, Philip Cornwall here. While Lee prepares for Ireland v South Africa, I am stepping in for the reaction to another fine England win. After all the flak Steve Borthwick took pre-tournament with suggestions he had lost the dressing room, what a November. The players rejected those claims verbally and have now demonstrated it in fine style.
79 mins. The ball is soon back in England hands, with Fisilau prominent in the carries moving them up to the 5 metre line. On an advantage Smith chips it in-goal but an All Black hand grounds it. However, we come back for the penalty.
78 mins. The scrum on halfway from the Barrett knock-on takes a few moments to complete, and when it does Marcus Smith boots the ball aimlessly back to NZ.
76 mins. England's forwards drive into the line with a few carries, but Scott Barrett gets amongst the breakdown to win a holding on penalty. The ball is cleared upfield and on the next possession Chessum rattles Barrett's torso to send the ball flying from his hands.
68 mins. As you can imagine the All Blacks are forcing it now, with the latest possession being shovelled to the right and into touch in the face of a white wall that remains unhurried and unmoved.
The most worrying thing if you are a New Zealander is how utterly weak they have looked. The energy is low which is likely a confidence thing, but their weak physicality is a real concern.
63 mins. Ellis Genge is off the bench and having a wonderful time running with the ball. His latest punches a hole into the 22 and a calm reset sends the ball to Atkinson to dive over in the right 13 channel.
60 mins. Aumua is on at hooker but the outcome remains the ball being chucked to an England player in the linout. The All Blacks have now lost 40% of their lineouts in this game; there really are no words.
58 mins. NZ are working phases near halfway where their initial pass is always 10 metres from the ruck to first receiver, and the England defenders are absolutely gobbling this maladroit nonsense up. In the end McKenzie has had enough and chips it forward for Barrett to chase, but the ball is gathered by England and that's that.
PENALTY! England 27 - 12 New Zealand (Marcus Smith)
55 mins. After that brief hiatus England return to the NZ 22, Early carrying strongly once more. They are up to the 5m line with the noise raising and that weirdly appropriated slave spiritual song ringing out from the crowd.
The All Blacks again do enough to spoil the possession at the ruck close to the line, but they were offside amongst it all and Marcus Smith caresses it over.
TRY! England 24 - 12 New Zealand (Beauden Barrett)
52 mins. And just like that, when all looked to be achieving nowt, there is a spring forward from the All Blacks with Roigard breaking the line and then finding Barrett on a fabulous angle from deep to outpace Furbank and race over from 30 metres.
50 mins. Eight phases from NZ near halfway go nowhere as the Cardiff vibe of of one-out runs, slow passes and zero disguise allow England to defend easily,
46 mins. Vaa'i charges down a van Poortvliet kick on the England 5m line, looping the ball high but into the arms of Chessum who carries forward to allow space for a successful clearance this time.
45 mins. The All Blacks wake up a bit, finding Beauden Barrett out on the right touchline who bunts the ball forward up the line, but the covering defenders mop it up.
43 mins. From the stolen lineout England move forward quickly before the ball moves left via a lovely looping pass from Fin Smith to Chessum, lurking like a mobile monolith on the wing. He rides a tackle and gets it down.
42 mins. Van Poortvliet puts the ball into touch after receiving the kick-off and Coles gets up in front of Holland to nick Taylor's lineout throw. Next lineout the same happens but it's Chessum who steals it.
It appears the "no more mistakes, eh lads?" plea from Rennie at half time has fallen on stony ears.
